title: 🔮 Prediction Strategies for Listening

sections.heading: Why prediction works
sections.body:
Your brain processes language faster when it knows what's coming. Prediction "primes" your ears for specific vocabulary, helping you catch answers even through accents, speed, or background noise.

Before each section, use the 30-second reading time to predict:
• What TYPE of information fills each gap (date? price? person's name?)
• What VOCABULARY you might hear in this context
• What potential DISTRACTORS might try to mislead you

sections.heading: Types of prediction
sections.body:
Grammar prediction: "The _____ was damaged" → noun needed
Context prediction: Registration form → expect names, dates, addresses
Logic prediction: "The cheapest option is the _____" → price or product name
Distractor prediction: "I said Tuesday... no, I mean Thursday" → the second answer

highlight: You can predict answer TYPE for 90% of gaps. "Name:", "Date:", "£___" are obvious. Even "Method: _____" tells you a noun or gerund is coming. This alone saves precious seconds.

instruction: Match each gap type to the prediction it needs:
explanation: Training yourself to predict answer types automatically — before the audio plays — is a Band 8+ listening technique. It reduces cognitive load during listening so you can focus on accuracy.

question: A question reads: "The lecturer argues that the MAIN reason for the decline was ___." Which prediction is most useful?
options: It could be anything — don't predict
Predict a noun or noun phrase describing a cause
correct: Predict a noun or noun phrase describing a cause
explanation:
"MAIN reason" → you're looking for a cause/factor
"Was ___" → needs a noun phrase (e.g. "habitat loss", "climate change", "economic pressure")

Knowing this, you can ignore answers that are dates, names, or verbs. Your brain narrows its focus to cause-related nouns — much more efficient.
